answer.text: For our final-year group project, four of us built a self-service GPU job runner for the department's machine learning teaching cluster.
The runner queued students' training jobs on Kubernetes (k3s) across six lab workstations with GPUs.
When jobs started failing, I found the cause by reading dmesg on the nodes.
I also wrote the per-course quota check in our scheduler extender.
The most interesting lesson came from that failure: the default /dev/shm in the pods was 64 MB, so the PyTorch data loaders crashed.
It taught me to check the node's kernel log first, because dmesg showed the OOM kills straight away and we lost two days before looking.
If I started again, I would put memory limits and a /dev/shm check into our job template from day one.
I would also set up node log alerts before launch, because we only found the OOM kills after students had lost work.

letter.text: I am applying for the Graduate Software Engineer, Drivers and Utilities 2027 role.
In my final-year group project, four of us built a self-service GPU job runner for our department's machine learning teaching cluster.
When jobs started failing, I traced the crashes through dmesg to a 64 MB /dev/shm in the pods.
By the spring term, 140 students were using it, and the average wait for a GPU had fallen from about two days to under 20 minutes.
I enjoyed the infrastructure side of that project more than the machine learning side, and Graphcore builds both the hardware and the cloud platform that models run on.
Thank you for considering my application.
